Deep dives / Americas

THE SPREAD OF PEOPLES · DEEP DIVE

Pictographs, Petroglyphs & Painted Caves of North America

Across every physiographic zone of North America, Indigenous peoples left dense visual histories etched into volcanic basalt, painted beneath high sandstone alcoves, modeled into deep pitch-black cave mud, and scraped into desert gravels. Far from anonymous scratches, these sites connect directly to Numic, Puebloan, Fremont, Cochimí, Olmec, Maya, Niitsítapi, Anishinaabe, Cherokee, Makah, Tlingit and Mississippian traditions.

Catalogs 71 map-pinned sites across 8 regions using approximate archaeological intervals (Benson et al., Steelman et al., Pederson et al., Diaz-Granados et al., Simek et al., NPS, BLM and UNESCO dossiers).

In Toto Specimen Archive · Visual records from caves to open overhangs

Filter verified open-licensed field photographs across traditions, media, and settings—from deep Paleolithic painted caverns like Lascaux and Chauvet to high-desert Nevada overhangs, Saharan canyons, Southern African shelters, and early stone settlements. Dates on rock art are approximate envelopes established by stratigraphy, luminescence, tufa carbonate, or pigment AMS analysis.

Nevada Overhangs & Great Basin Horizons

Starting along receding Lake Lahontan shorelines at Winnemucca Lake (~14,800–10,500 cal BP) and continuing through Grimes Point, Toquima Cave, Lagomarsino Canyon, Hickison Summit, Pahranagat Valley, Sloan Canyon, Valley of Fire and Gold Butte, Great Basin artists used intimate volcanic tuff overhangs, basalt talus ridges and Aztec sandstone seams overlooking scarce mountain springs. [1] [10] [2]

Regional Styles from Baja Caverns to Dark-Zone Caves

Farther east and south, artists shifted media dramatically with geology: glowing polychrome hematite, gypsum and black mineral paint across Chumash, Lower Pecos and Baja California canyon overhangs; monumental earth-scraped intaglios along Lower Colorado desert terraces; red iron-oxide Mishipeshu cliffs painted from canoes across the Canadian Shield; and deep underground Mississippian clay drawings lit solely by burning rivercane torches in Tennessee, Missouri and Alabama karst. [4] [5] [6] [7]

Cultural Attributions Across North America

In the main #explore map (filterable under 'Rock art & visual records'), all 71 newly added North American rock-art entries carry explicit attribution to their documented Indigenous makers and heritage traditions while honestly retaining approximate intervals. [8] [11]
